Extract 1. Questions 1-12. You hear a doctor in the A&E talking to a patient named Mandy Johnson.
For questions 1-12, complete the notes with a word or short phrase.
You now have 30 seconds to look at the notes.
Thank you.
So, Mrs Johnson, it looks like you're starting to feel a bit better from when the paramedics brought you in.
Oh yes, definitely. It was awful at first, but now I'm feeling much more oriented in time and place than I did then.
So tell me a bit about what has brought you here today.
Hmm, well, I don't remember much about the actual incident, but from what I understand, a colleague of mine saw me holding my head and then losing consciousness,
causing me to hit the front of my head against my desk.
The paramedics told me that my colleague said that my whole body began jerking
and he was unable to rouse me.
It sure gave him quite a shock, I can tell you that.
Then I guess the jerking stopped and I began making incomprehensible sounds
and not opening my eyes.
Yes, I can see the bruising on your forehead and a small laceration on your left cheek.
That must have happened during the episode.
Did you experience any symptoms in the hours or minutes before the episode?
Um, yes, I do remember. I had a terrible headache, worse than anything I've ever experienced.
It came on very suddenly and it felt like the headache was everywhere and not in just one spot on my head.
And what about any sensory disturbance or weakness before or after the event?
I don't recall any weakness or numbness. However, I did notice that I'd lost control of my bladder afterwards.
Episodes of incontinence are normal in these circumstances.
OK, and have you experienced a loss of consciousness or seizures in the past?
I've never had seizures or anything like this in the past, including episodes of losing consciousness.
And no recent head trauma?
Absolutely not. I mean, I woke up this morning feeling fine. I even bike to work, as I often do.
And Mrs Johnson, I know you are feeling a bit better now, but is the headache still present?
I still have a mild generalised headache and some nausea.
I've vomited twice, but the nurses have just given me some anti-sickness medication,
so hopefully that's stopped now.
What about visual disturbances like decreased acuity or tunnel vision?
I haven't noticed any visual problems, but my neck is killing me though.
It's quite stiff.
I'm not sure if it's because I've been lying in an awkward position or what.
Well, let's see.
Try to touch your chin to your chest.
Ouch, that's quite painful. Can't quite get there.
And I know you said you hadn't suffered any head trauma recently
and that this is the first time you have had something like this.
But I want to go a bit into your medical history to see if it can help us out.
Well, I can tell you that I don't have any medical problems
and I'm not currently on any medications.
I do smoke 10 cigarettes a day, a 20-year habit,
but I try to make up for that by not drinking any alcohol.
So I'm not sure if the nurses mentioned this,
but the next step here is to send you up for a CT scan
because of the loss of consciousness and headache.
So any idea of what?

Extract 2.
Questions 13 to 24.
You hear a GP talking to a patient about a diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome.
For questions 13 to 24, complete the notes with a word or short phrase.
You now have 30 seconds to look at the notes.
Welcome Mr Thomas, how are you feeling today?
Well, about the same as last time.
So, well, let's just take a few moments to review your symptoms before getting to the investigation results.
Yes, so I mentioned last time I thought I had gained some weight and it appears to keep going.
I mean, now my face has become very round and I have this, what I think is a fatty deposit between my shoulders.
It's not a good time for my body image.
And what about the stretch marks that you started noticing a bit before our last appointment?
Yes, that is still there and now it has spread up my abdomen and down my thighs.
I've also noticed that a cut I got working outside is taking forever to heal.
I'm not sure if that is related to all of this, but it is quite alarming.
And in general, what is your energy level and your mood like?
Some days I am not sure if it is severe fatigue or depression or a bit of both.
But there is a real struggle to get out of bed these days.
Also, I'm somewhat afraid to be around my grandchildren because I just feel so irritable all of the time.
I mean, the other day I lost my temper over the simplest thing.
I see. So it seems like your physical symptoms are definitely getting worse and these are affecting your mood somewhat.
I think that is definitely true. So what about those investigations, Doc?
Well, as you probably recall, we carried out quite a few diagnostic investigations.
There were the urine and blood tests.
With the urine tests, we were particularly interested in the cortisol levels.
We also had you help us conduct a saliva test to check for cortisol levels as well.
Yes, that was a bit intense, collecting urine over a 24-hour period and then having to remember to get a sample of saliva in the evening.

Yes, so the 24-hour urinary cortisol investigation showed cortisol excretion of more than three times the upper limit of normal, which is strongly suggestive of Cushing's syndrome, the late-night salivary cortisol measurement confirming this finding.
Okay, so I understand the high levels of cortisol and now you're saying they cause Cushing's syndrome?
What does cortisol do exactly?
Well, cortisol plays a variety of roles in your body.
For example, it helps to regulate blood pressure, reduces inflammation and keeps your heart and blood vessels functioning normally.
It also helps your body respond to stress.
Sounds like serious stuff.
It is. The condition is associated with significant morbidity and mortality.
So rapid diagnosis and management are essential.
What exactly would happen without treatment?
Well, there would be bone loss, which could result in unusual bone fractures,
and also high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes.
Other possibilities include frequent and unusual infections and a loss of muscle mass and strength.
I see. So what causes something like this, Cushing's syndrome?
Well, there are a few different causes, but the most common cause is the use of corticosteroids
like hydrocortisone or prednisone over an extended period of time.
However, we can rule out corticosteroids in your case because you are not on this type of medication.
That leaves your body's own overproduction of cortisol.
This is also known as endogenous Cushing's syndrome.
Here there are still a few possibilities, including a pituitary gland tumour,
an ACTH secreting tumour or a primary adrenal gland disease.
And so how do you find out which one is causing my problem?
Well, there are a few more investigations to be done.
First of all, one to detect plasma ACTH.
It is also necessary to get an MRI of the pituitary and a CT of the chest and abdomen.
These will help us to identify the presence of a tumour.
So now that you have me all scared, what are the treatment options?
Well, that will depend on the cause,
but there are medications that can be used to temporarily reduce your glucocortisoid levels,
which would help prepare you for definitive therapy.
Surgical management is a likely option,
particularly if the cause of your Cushing's syndrome is an adrenal or pituitary tumour.
That is the end of Part A. Now look at Part B.

You hear part of a training on suture materials.

Oftentimes when a junior surgical trainees ask what suture he would like for skin,
a common response is what the boss likes to use.
The answer has a number of purposes, to maintain the status quo and to cover up the fact that
many of us have only a very basic understanding of suture materials.
So that's exactly what today's session is about.
Why different suture materials are used and why it matters.
So suture types are broadly split into the following categories.
Absorbable versus non-absorbable.
Braided versus non-braided.
And natural versus synthetic.
So for the first category, absorbable sutures are broken down by the body over time by processes like hydrolysis and enzymatic degradation.
The amount of time this requires depends on the material as well as the location of insertion and the individual patient characteristics.
For example, the absorption rate of suture can increase in patients with ongoing infection, fever or protein deficiency.
So skin closures of a clean wound are mostly commonly achieved with this type of suture
as it provides soft tissue approximation to aid the healing process without permanent implantation of a foreign tissue.
However, not all absorbable sutures are created equally.
So the most commonly used...

Yes, his deltoid was a bit bruised.

Hello everyone, I want to start off today's briefing by reviewing some basic safety recommendations

they may not be able to get our attention quickly enough. So next

Hello everyone and welcome to today's programme. I'm very happy that we have Dr Christina Salem
with us to shed some light on a very important topic, diabetes and COVID-19. Welcome Dr Salem.
It's an honour to be here, especially to talk about such an essential and timely topic.
I mean, there has been so much on the news about this topic and it's often hard to get the answers that are important to patients.
Definitely. Filtering through all of the information can be overwhelming.
OK, so let's jump right in. We asked our viewers to send in their most pressing questions about the topic.
And so I want to start with the one that is on everybody's mind.
Are people with diabetes more likely to get COVID-19?
At this point, there is not enough data to show whether people with diabetes are more likely to get COVID-19.
In general, there is so much we do not know.
But the problem seems to be for patients with diabetes is worse outcomes, not a greater chance of contracting the virus.
For example, in China, where many cases have occurred, people with diabetes had much higher rates of serious complications and death than people without diabetes.
Overall, we believe that the more comorbidities someone has, for example, diabetes and heart
disease, the higher their chance of getting serious complications with COVID-19.
Interesting point about comorbidities in general.
Why exactly are people with diabetes more likely to experience serious complications?
Well, in general, diabetic people are more likely to experience severe symptoms and complications
when infected with any virus.
In addition, when people do not manage their diabetes well and experience fluctuating blood sugars, they are at risk for a number of diabetes-related complications.
And having these complications in addition to diabetes could worsen their chances of getting seriously ill from COVID-19 because their body's ability to fight off infection is compromised.
Another point is that viral infection can increase inflammation or internal swelling in people with diabetes.
This is also caused by above-target blood sugars, and both could contribute to more severe complications.
What about diabetic ketoacidosis? Do patients with diabetes need to be concerned about DKA?
When sick with a viral infection, people with diabetes do face an increased risk of DKA, commonly experienced by people with type 1 diabetes.
Also, DKA can make it challenging to manage fluid intake and electrolyte levels,
which is super important in managing sepsis.
I say this because sepsis and septic shock are some of the more serious complications
that some people with COVID-19 have experienced.
Speaking of type 1 diabetes, are the risks different for people with type 1 and type 2 diabetes?
We don't know of any reason to think COVID-19 will pose a difference in risk
between type 1 and type 2 diabetes. More important is that people with either type of diabetes vary
in their age, complications and how well they've been managing their diabetes. This last point of
management is key because like I previously mentioned what we do know is that people who
already have diabetes related health problems are likely to have worse outcomes if they contract
COVID-19 than people with diabetes who are otherwise healthy, whichever type of diabetes
they have. So if a person with diabetes suspects they have COVID-19, what do you recommend that
they do? Well, the first thing is to know the potential symptoms, which include fever, dry
cough and shortness of breath. If you feel like you are developing symptoms, call your doctor.

When you make that call, you should have a couple of things on hand, your glucose and ketone readings available, a report of your fluid consumptions, a clear idea and description of your symptoms, as well as specific questions on how to manage your diabetes.
One concern that many diabetics have, especially in light of recent issues with the availability of insulin and other diabetic supplies, is if or how COVID-19 will impact access to these supplies.
At this point, leading manufacturers are reporting that COVID-19 is not having an impact on their current manufacturing and distribution capabilities for insulin and other supplies at this time.
Organisations like the American Diabetes Association are continuing to monitor the situation and will provide updates should anything change.
The most important thing at this moment when so many people are out of work and struggling
is to know that there is also assistance for anyone struggling to pay for insulin.
All you need to do is contact.

So before we get started, I just wanted to introduce myself and talk a bit about the
importance of having mental health training as part of your medical education.
So I am Dr. Samuel Adams and I am a psychiatrist who is often involved in admitting patients
to the hospital for emergency mental health intervention.
Over the last few years, there has been a marked increase in patients coming into A&Es
with an acute need for mental health treatment.
However, many A&E doctors are not trained to carry out suicidal risk assessment,
meaning that many of these patients fall through the cracks.
So now let's talk about the suicidal risk assessment itself.
As with any patient interaction, it's key to try to establish rapport with the patient
early on in the interaction as this will allow you to perform an accurate assessment of their
mental health. This should include introducing yourself and explaining why you are seeing the
patient. The patient may also appreciate at this stage an acknowledgement that what you want to
talk about with them can sometimes be difficult and that it is confidential. Finally it is helpful
to keep in mind the main objectives of a suicide risk assessment which are to establish the patient's
intent, assess the seriousness and perceived seriousness of their attempt, and assess how
they feel about the attempt at the time of their assessment. So in order to try and establish intent,
it can be useful to start off with a day in question and obtain a narrative or an autobiographical
timeline of what happened. It is best to start this with open questions and then later use closed
questions for clarification. So now we are going to go into different questions and themes that
need to be covered in all scenarios to assess suicidal risk. So the first scenario we are going
to focus on is self-harm. So it's best to think about episodes of self-harm in terms of before,
during, and after. While asking a patient about what happened before an episode, we can focus on
the existence of any precipitant, such as an argument with a parent or a recent bereavement.
Another main area to focus on is whether the episode was planned or impulsive. Actions that
may help you to determine that or whether or not the patient carried out any final acts such as
writing a suicide note or terminating contracts for electricity or whether or not the patient
took any precautions against discovery like closing curtains, locking doors, waiting until
they knew everyone would be out of the house or going somewhere very remote. When it comes to
during an episode you should ask about the method of self-harm that was involved. What was going
through their mind at that time or whether or not they thought their self-harm would kill them.
Common types of self-harm include overdose, cutting, burning and attempted hanging.
You will want to adapt your questions at this point in the assessment to ask specifically
about the method of self-harm used. For example, for an overdose you will want to focus on how
they got hold of the medication as well as what they thought taking the amount of medication
would do. As far as after the episode, you can focus on how the patient reached out for help
and how they felt when help arrived. Also, in A&E setting, you can talk about how the patient feels
about the attempt now and what their current mood is. You might go through different scenarios with
the patient, such as if they were to go home today, what would they do or what might prevent
them from doing this again in the future? Once you have covered current and previous episodes of
self-harm. You should go into their past medical, drugs such as negative reactions they have had to
or ones they could overdose on, as well as family and social history. The last of which is very
important for checking epidemiological risk factors. An important aspect here to keep in mind,
you do elicit risks, then it is important to do something about it, such as if there is a child
safeguarding concern. This needs to be shared with a senior nurse or consultant so it can be addressed.
Areas to be covered in a social history include living situation,
occupation, alcohol consumption and the use of recreational drug use.
At this point, you as a physician will need to make a decision.
In most cases, you will have a conversation to agree on a management plan.
For patients who are not suicidal and who you intend to send home,
you should realize you may be sending them home with no follow-up
or support from mental health services.
In this case, a safety plan should include reaching out for support from family and friends,
recognising stressors, avoiding harmful alcohol use when stressed
and suggesting they see a GP and contact local mental health services that see people who self-refer.
